title: At the market
goal: Bargain, ask prices, and count to a hundred — while turning one thinking habit around: Pashto says the units first, then the tens.
bekal: ask prices and bargain without sounding rude
count 20–100 with the units before the tens

dialogs.title: خبرې اترې — د مېوو په دکان کې
dialogs.intro: The old bazaar in the middle of Kabul. Pomegranates, grapes, and melons piled chest-high. Najib lets Budi do the bargaining himself.

lines.speaker: بودي:
lines.text: سلام. زه انګور غواړم. څومره دی؟
lines.baca: salām. zə angūr ghwāṛəm. tsomra day?
lines.id: Hello. I'd like some grapes. How much are they?
lines.literal: salaam. I grapes want-I. how-much is?

lines.speaker: بودي:
lines.text: اویا؟ ډېره ګرانه ده. پنځوس څنګه؟
lines.baca: awyā? ḍera grāna da. pindzos tsənga?
lines.id: Seventy? That's very expensive. How about fifty?
lines.literal: seventy? very expensive is. fifty how?

lines.speaker: دوکاندار:
lines.id: Fifty is impossible. Make it sixty.

lines.speaker: بودي:
lines.id: OK, sixty. Give me two kilos.

lines.speaker: دوکاندار:
lines.text: دوه کیلو یو سل او شل افغانۍ. بل څه؟
lines.baca: dwa kīlo yaw sal aw shəl afghānəy. bəl tsə?
lines.id: Two kilos is a hundred and twenty afghanis. Anything else?
lines.literal: two kilos one hundred and twenty afghani. other what?

lines.speaker: دوکاندار:
lines.text: هو، د کندهار انار. ډېر خوږ دی.
lines.baca: ho, də Kandahār anār. ḍer khwaẓ day.
lines.literal: yes, of Kandahar pomegranates. very sweet are.

lines.speaker: دوکاندار:
lines.text: پنځه اتیا افغانۍ. خو تاسو مېلمه یاست — اویا وکړئ.
lines.baca: pindzə atyā afghānəy. kho tāso melma yāst — awyā wəkṛəy.
lines.id: Five are eighty afghanis. But you're a guest — make it seventy.
lines.literal: five eighty afghani. but you(pl) guest are — seventy do-you(pl).

lines.speaker: بودي:
lines.text: ډېره مننه! تاسو ډېر مهربان یاست.
lines.baca: ḍera manana! tāso ḍer mihrabān yāst.
lines.id: Thank you very much! You're very kind.
lines.literal: much thanks! you(pl) very kind are.

lines.speaker: دوکاندار:
lines.text: دا زمونږ دود دی. مېلمه د خدای دی.
lines.baca: dā zmūẓ dod day. melma də khudāy day.
lines.id: It's our custom. A guest belongs to God.
lines.literal: this of-us custom is. guest of God is.

lines.speaker: بودي:
lines.id: How much is it all together?

lines.speaker: دوکاندار:
lines.text: یو سل او نوي افغانۍ. په خیر ولاړ شئ!
lines.baca: yaw sal aw nawī afghānəy. pə khayr wlāṛ shəy!
lines.id: A hundred and ninety afghanis. Have a good trip!
lines.literal: one hundred and ninety afghani. with goodness leave become-you(pl)!

notes: Bargaining in Afghanistan is not an argument but a conversation, and refusing to bargain is actually seen as odd. A safe pattern: name a figure about two-thirds of the asking price, then meet in the middle. The key phrase ډېره ګرانه ده (that's far too expensive) is said with a smile, not a frown.

The word ګرانه deserves attention because it has two meanings at once. The word ګران means "expensive" and also "dear, beloved" — the greeting ګرانه دوسته means "dear friend", much like English *dear* once meant both. Context separates them, and nobody is ever confused.

Look at the numbers اویا (seventy) and شپېته (sixty) in the dialogue. Both are separate words to be learned, just like the tens. The ones with a pattern are the compound numbers such as اته ویشت (28) and پنځه څلوېښت (45).

The phrase نه کېږي literally means "it doesn't become", and it means "it can't be done" or "impossible". It is the gentlest refusal in Pashto, much softer than saying نه outright, and shopkeepers use it all day long.

The sentence مېلمه د خدای دی — "a guest belongs to God" — is not just sales talk. It is part of مېلمستیا, the duty of hospitality that is one of the pillars of the Pashtun code of life. If you look foreign and make an effort to speak Pashto, you will often get the guest price, and refusing it would cause offense.
The farewell په خیر ولاړ شئ means "go with goodness". The reply is په مخه دې ښه or simply مننه. You will hear it every time you leave a shop, a house, or a shared taxi.

grammars.title: ⚠️ Numbers 20–100: units first, tens second
body: This is the thinking habit you have to turn around. The number 28 in Pashto is اته ویشت, literally "eight twenty". Speakers say the units first, just like German and Dutch, and the reverse of English.
⚠️ Note one change of form: twenty on its own is **شل** *shəl*, but as soon as a unit stands in front of it, it becomes **ویشت** *wisht*. No other ten changes shape like that.

grammars.title: Asking prices and bargaining
body: The price question always uses څومره, not څو. The word څو counts things one by one; څومره asks about amounts of money, weight, distance, and any size that is not counted in units.
Notice that the answer uses the plural verb دي if the thing is plural: پنځه انار څومره **دي**؟ For one thing, use دی or ده according to its gender.

blocks.text: Afghanistan is famous across Asia for its fruit, and the market is the best place to practice numbers. Some of the names below may ring a bell — *bādām* and *kishmish* are the same words in Urdu and Hindi, and *zardālū* reached Spanish as *albaricoque* — and that is no coincidence: they all traveled the same trade routes.

blocks.title: Measures and money
items: Weight uses **کیلو** *kīlo* and **سېر** *ser*, an old unit still used in villages and roughly equal to seven kilograms.
The currency is the **افغانۍ** *afghānəy*, and it is a feminine word — so the price is said اویا افغانۍ **ده**, not دی.
In the border areas of Pakistan the **روپۍ** *rūpəy* is used, the same word as the Indian *rupee*, and also feminine.
Half is **نیم** *nīm* for masculine things and **نیمه** *nīma* for feminine ones: نیم کیلو (half a kilo).
⚠️ The word **بیه** *bīya* means price, and **قیمت** *qīmat* is also used, especially in cities. Both are correct.

blocks.title: Phrases that save a bargaining session
items: To open: دا څومره دی؟ or بیه یې څومره ده؟
To bargain without being rude: ډېره ګرانه ده، ارزانه کړئ *ḍera grāna da, arzāna kṛəy*.
To close: ښه، منم *ṣa, manəm* — "OK, I accept".
To back out politely: بیا راځم *byā rādzəm* — "I'll come back". This phrase often brings the price down before you have even taken a step.
⚠️ Don't bargain over bread, tea, or ready-made food. Bargaining is for goods, not for food that has already been cooked.
